Passage – 1


The ancient Greek physician Hippocrates defined health as a body in balance. The human body was a system of four coordinated
humours (blood, black bile, yellow bile, phlegm), each of which had its own balance of qualities (hot or cold, wet or dry) connected to the
four elements (fire, air, earth, water). The balance of these qualities and humours was inextricably linked to environmental conditions.
Phlegm, for instance, was connected to the element of water, and had the qualities of cold and wet. Hippocrates recognised that when this
bodily system was exposed to conditions that perturbed or exacerbated its humours, such as the cold and wet of a snowstorm, the
system became unbalanced, in this case producing too much phlegm. His treatments for an abundance of phlegm focused on removing
the excess humour and increasing the yellow bile (hot and dry) to bring the body back into balance.
Today, we might identify such a condition as a respiratory disease. Hippocrates would not have identified the condition so locally. He
would have considered it a condition of the whole body: 'dis-ease' was literally a system out of ease or balance.


Today we think less about the whole body as a complex system and more about its parts and sub-systems. An X-ray of the lungs shows
congestion, so we assume the problem is in the lungs and treat for pneumonia, not worrying about other parts of the body unless they
show their own symptoms. If a culture in the pathology lab shows a particular microbe at work, we prescribe the relevant antibiotics to
combat that microbe rather than attempt to rebalance the system as a whole. This move toward localised diagnoses began in the 18th
century with the rise of morbid anatomy and the localisation of symptoms to parts. The French physician René Laënnec's invention of the
stethoscope in 1816 allowed him to hear various abnormal sounds in the chest of a patient suffering respiratory distress.


The result was the localisation of abnormalities to particular parts of the body, which led to the concept of localised diseases and the need
for specialised treatments. Modern medicine celebrates the ability to diagnose problems based on localisation of symptoms. The
systemic imbalance or 'dis-ease' of Hippocrates thus became a growing set of separate diseases associated with specific causes,
dissociated from the notion of the body as a system. Following the localisation of diseases came the specialisation of treatments. These
treatments typically rely on identifying the problem within a particular part or subsystem and fixing it, with the goal of getting the patient
back to 'normal'.


Despite vast differences in understanding of disease and treatments, models of health from Hippocrates to modern medicine have
focused on reestablishing the same state as occurred before illness. Health is a concept imbued with a sense of stability; it is constituted
by a body returning to a state that existed before disease or injury and the maintenance of this state. Stability is therefore understood as
the maintenance or regeneration of a single, 'healthy' state of the body.


(507 words, Source: Aeon Essays)

Passage – 2


There are no borders here to divide fresh water from salt, river from sea. The tides reach as far as two hundred miles inland and every day
thousands of acres of forest disappear underwater, only to reemerge hours later. The currents are so powerful as to reshape the islands
almost daily - some days the water tears away entire promontories and peninsulas; at other times it throws up new shelves and
sandbanks where there were none before.


When the tides create new land, overnight mangroves begin to gestate, and if the conditions are right they can spread so fast as to cover a
new island within a few short years. A mangrove forest is a universe unto itself, utterly unlike other woodlands or jungles. There are no
towering, vine- looped trees, no ferns, no wildflowers, no chattering monkeys or cockatoos. Mangrove leaves are tough and leathery, the
branches gnarled and the foliage often impassably dense. Visibility is short and the air still and fetid. At no moment can human beings
have any doubt of the terrain's hostility to their presence, of its cunning and resourcefulness, of its determination to destroy or expel them.
Every year, dozens of people perish in the embrace of that dense foliage, killed by tigers, snakes and crocodiles.


There is no prettiness here to invite the stranger in: yet to the world at large this archipelago is known as the Sundarbans, which means
"the beautiful forest." There are some who believe the word to be derived from the name of a common species of mangrove - the sundari
tree, Heriteria minor.


But the word's origin is no easier to account for than is its present prevalence, for in the record books of the Mughal emperors this region
is named not in reference to a tree but to a tide - bhati. And to the inhabitants of the islands this land is known as bhatir desh - the tide
country - except that bhati is not just the "tide" but one tide in particular, the ebb tide, the bhata. This is a land half submerged at high tide:
it is only in falling that the water gives birth to the forest. To look upon this strange parturition, midwifed by the moon, is to know why the
name "tide country" is not just right but necessary. For as with Rilke's catkins hanging from the hazel and the spring rain upon the dark
earth, when we behold the lowering tide we, who have always thought of joy as rising . . . feel the emotion that almost amazes us when a
happy thing falls.

(431 words, Source: Amitav Ghosh - The Hungry Tide)

When I wrote my first novel, The House With a Thousand Stories, I drew inspiration not only from great 20th-century novels like Toni
Morrison's Song of Solomon and important Indian English novels like Amitav Ghosh's The Shadow Lines, but also from fiction written in
the regional languages of India. My first language is Assamese but I also know how to read Bangla and Hindi. At home, we had a large
stock of Bangla, Assamese, and some English books. The library I regularly visited had delicious thrillers written in Hindi that I devoured
during summer vacations. All of these languages translated world classics, too. I read most of the great Russian novels in Assamese,
some British and American classics by Twain and Dickens in Hindi, Bengali, and Assamese. Perhaps this is why every time a Western
newspaper comes up with a recommended list of novels about India I find them insufficient. These lists always contain books written
originally in English. Due to British colonialism, there is no doubt a large body of important Indian literary works that are read globally are
written in English. But there is a problem here: only ten percent of India's population knows English, and this group of people gets to
represent India through their works.


The rest of India's population - who don't have the privilege of learning English or away from the wealthy metropolitan centers of
opportunities and thus English learning and discourse - read and write in one of the many official languages in India. India's constitution
lists 22 significant languages such as Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Tamil, Gujarati, Kashmiri, Hindi, etc. - and that's not including the
thousands of dialects and tribal languages in which people write as well. These languages have a long and continuous written tradition.
For instance, Assamese - my first language - has a literary tradition reaching back to the 5th century. With the arrival of print culture in the
modern period, Assamese literature, like all other Indian literary cultures, flourished. A large amount of this was anti-colonial literature that
led to the growth of nationalist consciousness and eventually contributed to British colonizers' ejection from India.


The colonial administration systematically tried to replace these strong literary cultures with English. But they failed. A complex body of
literature emerged from this linguistic violence on India's native intellectual culture and subsequent resistance. Modern Indian literature
draws nutrients not only from South Asia's indigenous traditions, but also from literary cultures in the U.K., Europe, Latin America, Russia,
China, and the United States. Hence, every time a Western publication makes a list of books from India and doesn't feature a single work
written in one of India's many languages, it reinforces colonial stereotypes and erodes the process of decolonization. It reestablishes the
hegemony of the English language and wipes the rich local traditions that are longer and richer.


The novels in this list - widely considered as modern Indian classics - attempt to challenge the Western stereotype that Indians primarily
read in English or that Indian literature is written predominantly in English. In fact, in the last two or three decades, the reading public has
shifted towards consuming more and more literary works translated from Indian languages. I also belong to a generation of new writers

from India who are comfortable writing in both English and a regional language. The future is at least bilingual, if not multilingual.

The world could be heading toward its worst energy crisis since the 1970s, with disruptions to oil, gas and critical commodities
intensifying amid the Middle East conflict, Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency, warned. Describing the situation as "very
severe", Birol said the scale of the shock now exceeds the twin oil crises of 1973 and 1979, as well as the gas market upheaval following
Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "This crisis… is now two oil crises and one gas crisis put all together," he said at the National Press Club of
Australia. The disruption has been driven largely by the near-complete halt of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global
energy flows that has been effectively blocked. The shutdown has triggered what the IEA describes as the largest-ever supply shock, with
Persian Gulf producers forced to lock in output or rely on limited alternative routes. "And not only oil and gas, some of the vital arteries of
the global economy… their trade is all interrupted," Birol said, pointing to disruptions in petrochemicals, fertilisers, sulphur and helium. He
stressed that reopening Hormuz remains the single most critical step. "The single most important solution to this problem is opening up
the Hormuz trade," he said. The crisis has also caused extensive damage to infrastructure across the region. "At least forty energy assets…
are severely or very severely damaged across nine countries," Birol noted, underlining the scale of the supply disruption. The IEA has
already overseen a historic release of about 400 million barrels from emergency reserves to stabilise markets, and Birol said more could
follow if needed. "If needed, we can put more oil in the markets… but this is not the solution. It will only help to reduce the pain," he said.
Birol warned that the fallout from the energy shock is now spilling over into the broader global economy. "The global economy is facing a
major, major threat today," he said, adding that "no country will be immune" if the crisis persists.

Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India enshrines a fundamental limitation on the State's power to impose criminal liability. It mandates
that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act, nor be
subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law then in force. The protection under Article 20(1)
operates in relation to substantive criminal law, and is directed against two forms of retrospective operation: first, the creation of criminal
offences ex post facto, and second, the aggravation of punishment retrospectively. The provision is thus rooted in the principle of fairness,
ensuring that individuals have notice of the legal consequences of their conduct at the time of acting.


However, the scope of Article 20(1) is not absolute. It does not extend to laws that are procedural in nature, even if such laws operate

retrospectively, unless such procedural alteration is so substantive in effect that it effectively alters the nature or degree of punishment.
Similarly, laws imposing civil liabilities or regulatory penalties-even if burdensome-are generally not within the ambit of Article 20(1), unless
they are, in substance, punitive and indistinguishable from criminal sanctions. Further complexity arises in the context of continuing
offences, where the wrongful conduct persists over a period of time. In such cases, a law enacted during the continuance of the offence
may validly apply to that portion of the conduct occurring after the law has come into force, without necessarily offending Article 20(1).

laws that are beneficial to the accused, such as those reducing punishment or decriminalizing conduct. The constitutional inquiry,
therefore, often turns on the true character of the law-whether it is substantive or procedural, civil or criminal, punitive or regulatory-and
whether its retrospective application results in a real and substantive disadvantage equivalent to enhanced punishment.

Under the Indian Penal Code, the distinction between culpable homicide and murder rests on the degree and certainty of intention and
knowledge accompanying the act causing death. Section 299 defines culpable homicide as causing death with the intention of causing
death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause
death.


Section 300 elevates culpable homicide to murder when the act is committed with a higher degree of certainty and intention. It identifies
circumstances where culpable homicide becomes murder, including:
(1) where there is intention to cause death;
(2) where there is intention to cause bodily injury which the offender knows to be likely to cause death;
(3) where the bodily injury intended is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death;
(4) where the act is so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death.


However, Section 300 also carves out exceptions, under which culpable homicide does not amount to murder, even if it otherwise satisfies
the conditions of murder. These include acts done under grave and sudden provocation, in the course of a sudden fight without
premeditation, in exceeding the right of private defence, or by a public servant acting in good faith but exceeding lawful authority. The
distinction is not merely between intention and knowledge, but between degrees of probability of death, and the specificity of injury
intended. While murder involves a definite or near-certain fatal consequence, culpable homicide may involve only a likelihood of death.
Similarly, the presence of exceptions does not negate culpability but reduces the offence from murder to culpable homicide not amounting
to murder. Courts have repeatedly emphasized that the determination depends on the totality of circumstances, including nature of
weapon used, part of body targeted, severity of blow, and surrounding facts indicating intention or knowledge.

Under the Indian Penal Code, the distinction between culpable homicide and murder rests on the degree and certainty of intention and
knowledge accompanying the act causing death. Section 299 defines culpable homicide as causing death with the intention of causing
death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause
death.


Section 300 elevates culpable homicide to murder when the act is committed with a higher degree of certainty and intention. It identifies
circumstances where culpable homicide becomes murder, including:
(1) where there is intention to cause death;
(2) where there is intention to cause bodily injury which the offender knows to be likely to cause death;
(3) where the bodily injury intended is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death;
(4) where the act is so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death.


However, Section 300 also carves out exceptions, under which culpable homicide does not amount to murder, even if it otherwise satisfies
the conditions of murder. These include acts done under grave and sudden provocation, in the course of a sudden fight without
premeditation, in exceeding the right of private defence, or by a public servant acting in good faith but exceeding lawful authority. The
distinction is not merely between intention and knowledge, but between degrees of probability of death, and the specificity of injury
intended. While murder involves a definite or near-certain fatal consequence, culpable homicide may involve only a likelihood of death.
Similarly, the presence of exceptions does not negate culpability but reduces the offence from murder to culpable homicide not amounting
to murder. Courts have repeatedly emphasized that the determination depends on the totality of circumstances, including nature of
weapon used, part of body targeted, severity of blow, and surrounding facts indicating intention or knowledge.

The determination of criminal liability of children under Indian law requires a layered analysis under the Juvenile Justice (Care and
Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act), read with principles of criminal law under the Indian Penal Code (IPC). While a "child" is any
person below 18 years, the law differentiates between categories of children based on age, nature of offence, and degree of mental
culpability.


Offences are classified into petty, serious, and heinous, with heinous offences being those carrying a minimum punishment of seven years
or more. In cases involving children aged 16-18 years accused of heinous offences, the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) must conduct a
preliminary assessment into (i) mental and physical capacity to commit the offence, (ii) ability to understand consequences, and (iii)
circumstances of commission.
This assessment is not a trial but a jurisdictional filter, determining whether the child should be subjected to adult criminal process.
Such transfer is exceptional, not routine. The law does not equate chronological age with adult culpability, nor does it permit substitution
of statutory criteria with societal perceptions of gravity or outrage. Failure to apply the correct parameters vitiates the transfer decision.


Parallelly, under the IPC, the doctrine of doli incapax introduces a graduated immunity: children below 7 are absolutely exempt, while those
between 7 and 12 are exempt only if they lack sufficient maturity to understand the nature and consequences of their act. This doctrine
concerns capacity to commit an offence, whereas the JJ Act concerns forum and manner of trial, though both may intersect.


Even where a child is tried as an adult, the JJ framework continues to influence sentencing architecture, ensuring that punishment is not
purely retributive. Thus, the inquiry is not binary but involves distinguishing between capacity, classification, procedural compliance, and
residual protection.

Section 4 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 governs the communication of proposals (offers), acceptances, and revocations, and
determines the exact moment at which each becomes complete. The provision introduces a deliberate asymmetry between the position
of the proposer and the acceptor.


The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Thus, mere dispatch of

an offer is insufficient; knowledge is essential.


However, communication of acceptance operates differently. As against the proposer, communication of acceptance is complete when it
is put into a course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the power of the acceptor. As against the acceptor, it is complete when it
comes to the knowledge of the proposer.


This creates a dual-timing rule: the proposer becomes bound earlier (on dispatch), while the acceptor becomes bound later (on receipt).


Revocation follows a similar dual structure. A proposal may be revoked at any time before communication of its acceptance is complete
as against the proposer, but not afterwards. Likewise, an acceptance may be revoked at any time before communication of acceptance is
complete as against the acceptor, but not afterwards.
Thus, an acceptance may be revoked even after it has been dispatched, provided the revocation reaches the proposer before the
acceptance itself comes to his knowledge.


The scheme of Section 4 therefore hinges on identifying:
(i) when knowledge is acquired,
(ii) when transmission becomes irreversible, and
(iii) the relative timing of acceptance and revocation.


In cases of instantaneous modes of communication, such as telephone, telex, or email, the rule differs. Communication of acceptance is
complete only when it is received by the proposer, as such modes do not involve any time lag between transmission and receipt.
Therefore, in such cases, the acceptor is bound only when the acceptance comes to the knowledge of the proposer, and the proposer
becomes bound at the same moment.


Further, acceptance must ordinarily be made in the same manner as the proposal is communicated, unless the proposer prescribes a
different mode or waives such requirement.

(iv) whether any exception applies.

The prospect of communicating with extraterrestrial intelligence has fascinated both scientists and writers, yet the frameworks guiding
this pursuit often reflect human assumptions more than objective possibility. Early speculative works imagined alien communication as
fundamentally different from human language, involving unfamiliar sensory modes or non-linear structures. In contrast, modern scientific
approaches tend to rely on models that resemble human cognition, implicitly assuming that alien beings would think and communicate in
comparable ways.


Such anthropocentric thinking imposes significant limitations. Efforts to detect extraterrestrial signals frequently depend on technologies
like radio transmission, presuming that alien civilizations would develop similar tools and use them in recognisable ways. This not only
narrows the search but also defines "communication" in strictly human terms, potentially excluding forms that do not align with our
expectations.


The continued absence of empirical evidence reinforces these concerns. Despite decades of systematic efforts, no confirmed
extraterrestrial signals have been identified. This silence challenges the assumption that intelligent life is both common and detectable.
Evolutionary theory further suggests that the emergence of human-like intelligence is shaped by highly specific conditions, making its
replication elsewhere uncertain rather than inevitable.


Even if extraterrestrial intelligence exists, meaningful communication may remain elusive. Some theories propose that mathematics or
logic could serve as universal languages, but these rely on the assumption that all intelligent beings perceive and structure reality similarly.
However, differences in perception or cognition could produce entirely distinct systems of meaning. Human difficulties in interpreting
animal communication or ancient symbolic scripts demonstrate how challenging understanding can be, even within familiar contexts.


Given these uncertainties, a more flexible approach may be necessary. Rather than projecting human models onto unknown forms of life,
the study of alien communication might benefit from considering radically different possibilities. In doing so, it not only broadens the
search for extraterrestrial contact but also deepens our understanding of the nature and limits of language itself.

A census survey conducted by the Regional Planning Authority in Shantipur District in 2023–24 revealed key insights into its demographic
and occupational structure. The total registered population was 5,500, comprising 3,100 females and 2,400 males. The survey was part of
a broader state government initiative aimed at assessing workforce distribution and designing targeted welfare schemes for
underrepresented groups across various sectors. Field officers visited households across 14 sub-districts to collect data on primary
occupations, age groups, and gender representation. A central committee later verified and compiled the collected information before its
official publication.


The findings categorized the workforce into five sectors: Agriculture, Manufacturing, Trade, Education, and Healthcare. Agriculture
employed 22% of the total population, with females accounting for 28% of the total female population. Manufacturing engaged 16% of the
population; however, only 12% of the total female population was employed in this sector. Trade accounted for 20% of the population, with
18% of the total female population participating in it. Education employed 18% of the population and had relatively higher female
participation, at 24% of the total female population. The remaining population was engaged in Healthcare.


The survey highlighted notable gender disparities, particularly in Manufacturing and Trade, where female participation remained low.
These findings prompted authorities to introduce targeted employment and skill development programs to improve female representation
in these sectors and promote inclusive workforce growth.
